newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel denies cancelling gas deal.
newsitem.headline: Israel denies cancelling gas deal.

text.p: Israeli Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon denied on Sunday Jordanian charges the Jewish state cancelled a joint venture that would have supplied the two countries with gas from the Gulf.

"Regarding cancellation of the Aqaba project which the Jordanian energy minister related to...Sharon emphasises Israel did not cancel any project and it is ready to discuss with any element the supplying of gas to Israel, including with...Qatar and Enron which proposed supplying liquefied gas.
"A letter clarifying this position was sent...to the Qatari foreign minister," Sharon's office said in a statement.

U.S. energy giant Enron Corp spearheaded the project to set up a $300 million regasification plant at Jordan's Red Sea port of Aqaba to bring liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Qatar to Israel and Jordan in the first quarter of 2001.
Sharon's office added: "In parallel, the Infrastructure Ministry continues to check various possibilities to bring natural gas and electricity on a cost benefit basis also from other sources."
Jordanian Energy Minister Hashem Dabbas told Reuters earlier on Sunday: "The project is non-existent...the new Israeli government is apparently not interested in the project any longer."
The deal was agreed at a Middle East economic summit two years ago following the Jordan-Israel peace treaty in 1994 that ended a 46-year state of war.

Israel's previous Labour government, ousted in elections last May, strongly lobbied for the project, despite opposition of some Israeli industrial groups, to help draw Jordan closer economically and consolidate peace.
Last October, Israel's Infrastructure Ministry said Israel had informed Enron Corp that it no longer had an exclusive agreement to negotiate with Qatar for natural gas supplies for Israel.

Enron and Israel signed a memorandum of understanding in October 1995 granting the Houston-based company 180 days to finalise an agreement with Qatar for the supply of at least two million tonnes a year of natural gas.
Dabbas said that Jordan's own letter of intent with Enron signed last March also lapsed after a 180-day period expired.
Investors in Jordan say Israel believes getting LNG from Qatar by vessels is more expensive than other sources including direct pumping of gas from Egypt.
They said the deal's collapse was a setback to efforts to create large private sector joint ventures that would create a common interest in preserving peace.
Sharon on Sunday emphasised the importance of such ventures.

"Israel sees great importance in furthering economic projects jointly between Israel and Jordan, including other projects in the area of production and use of electricity on the a basis beneficial to both sides," his office said.
